title: Lessons grounded in NCTM Effective Mathematics Teaching Practices emphasizing discourse, reasoning, and real-world connections
description: iRCL lessons are designed around the Effective Mathematics Teaching Practices from the National Council of Teachers of Mathematics. The page states lessons "emphasize discourse, reasoning, and real-world connections," and the program is closely aligned with grade-level standards and designed to support all learners, including those needing additional scaffolding.
requirements: Alignment with grade-level standards; print and digital materials including teacher guides and manipulatives
target_learners: K-8 mathematics students, including those who need additional scaffolding
examples: The program combines print and digital materials, including teacher guides, student workbooks, practice tools, and hands-on manipulatives

article_title: What Makes Something Hard(er)? Explaining Question Difficulty in Natural Language
citation: Peng Cui, Qiaoyuan Zheng, Rudolf Debelak, Mrinmaya Sachan. (2026). What Makes Something Hard(er)? Explaining Question Difficulty in Natural Language. Preprint. https://arxiv.org/abs/2610.01627
title: A three-step framework for generating validated natural-language explanations of question difficulty
description: The article introduces a framework that treats difficulty as "a quantity to be explained" rather than only estimated. It first fits a 1PL IRT model to LLM response matrices to estimate each item's difficulty, then repeatedly samples "contrastive sets of difficult and easy items" and prompts an LLM to propose hypotheses explaining the gap, and finally refines, matches, and selects hypotheses via L1-regularized regression on held-out questions. The output is interpretable natural-language difficulty factors that can be used predictively and causally.
requirements: Requires LLM response records for the question pool to fit the IRT model
Requires a held-out verification set for hypothesis selection via LASSO
constraints: Difficulty estimates depend on the respondent pool of LLMs used to fit the IRT model
target_learners: large language models evaluated on reasoning benchmarks
target_learning_goals: explaining and predicting item difficulty of reasoning questions
examples: Applied to GSM8K, BBH-structured, and WinoGrande with 5,000 or 3,811 LLM respondents per dataset
key_sources: Peng Cui, Qiaoyuan Zheng, Rudolf Debelak, Mrinmaya Sachan. (2026). What Makes Something Hard(er)? Explaining Question Difficulty in Natural Language. Preprint. https://arxiv.org/abs/2610.01627

article_title: Applying psychometric methods to distinguish between human and generative AI responses to multiple-choice assessments
citation: Alona Strugatski and Giora Alexandron. (2025). Applying Item Response Theory to Distinguish Between Human and Generative AI Responses to Multiple-Choice Assessments. LAK'25 pre-print. https://arxiv.org/abs/2412.02713
title: IRT-based person-fit statistics as a conceptual framework for distinguishing GenAI from human response patterns in MCQ assessment
description: The paper proposes applying Item Response Theory and, within it, Person-Fit Statistics to educational assessment as a lens for detecting GenAI cheating. PFS is "a collection of statistical methods designed to assess the alignment between an individual's test performance and an expected response pattern". Because AI and human intelligence differ architecturally, AI cheating manifests as deviations from expected human response patterns, quantified by non-parametric statistics (G, G*, U3, ZU3) computed per examinee. The framework grounds a learning-analytics approach in established educational measurement theory rather than ad-hoc detection heuristics.
requirements: Tests of at least 20 items, since short tests may not provide enough data to reliably detect aberrant patterns
Cheating must remain non-normative for aberrancy-based detection to work
constraints: Sensitive to the level of pollution
Applied retrospectively and less appropriate for real-time detection
High PFS misfit can also arise from legitimate conditions such as learning disabilities
target_learners: high-school students taking formative chemistry assessments
prospective students taking high-stakes entrance exams
target_learning_goals: valid assessment of learner ability on multiple-choice instruments
academic integrity of MCQ-based summative assessment
examples: The framework was instantiated on a 22-item chemistry diagnostic (931 respondents) and a 20-item psychometric quantitative chapter (over 4,800 respondents), with 20 runs each of ChatGPT-4o, Gemini 1.5 Pro, and Claude 3.5 Sonnet.
key_sources: Alona Strugatski and Giora Alexandron. (2025). Applying Item Response Theory to Distinguish Between Human and Generative AI Responses to Multiple-Choice Assessments. LAK'25 pre-print. https://arxiv.org/abs/2412.02713

article_title: Applying psychometric methods to distinguish between human and generative AI responses to multiple-choice assessments
citation: Alona Strugatski and Giora Alexandron. (2025). Applying Item Response Theory to Distinguish Between Human and Generative AI Responses to Multiple-Choice Assessments. LAK'25 pre-print. https://arxiv.org/abs/2412.02713
title: Two-instrument evaluation dataset: chemistry diagnostic and psychometric quantitative chapter with injected chatbot responses
description: The study's empirical base is a pair of authentic MCQ instruments from very different contexts. The first was "a chemistry diagnostic examination administered via a Moodle platform as a formative assessment activity" with 22 MCQs and 931 high-school respondents; the second was a 20-item quantitative chapter from a high-stakes psychometric entrance exam with over 4,800 respondents. Both are multi-modal, containing images/figures and formulas. GenAI responses were generated by running each of three premium chatbots 20 times per instrument as new sessions, with non-zero temperature, and non-answers counted as incorrect.
requirements: Instruments of at least 20 items for reliable aberrancy detection
Chat models supporting figures and visual modalities
constraints: Only two instruments and three specific GenAI tools, which the authors name as the main external-validity limitation
target_learners: high-school students preparing for matriculation tests
prospective higher-education students
target_learning_goals: measuring science and quantitative ability via MCQ assessment
examples: Each chatbot was run 20 times per instrument to mimic 20 cheating students, and 5%, 10%, and 25% pollution datasets were constructed by combining these responses with the appropriate number of human responses.
key_sources: Alona Strugatski and Giora Alexandron. (2025). Applying Item Response Theory to Distinguish Between Human and Generative AI Responses to Multiple-Choice Assessments. LAK'25 pre-print. https://arxiv.org/abs/2412.02713

article_title: A Meta-Analysis of Single Case Research Studies on Aided Augmentative and Alternative Communication Systems with Individuals with Autism Spectrum Disorders
citation: Ganz, J. B., Earles-Vollrath, T. L., Heath, A. K., Parker, R. I., Rispoli, M. J., & Duran, J. B. (2012). A Meta-Analysis of Single Case Research Studies on Aided Augmentative and Alternative Communication Systems with Individuals with Autism Spectrum Disorders. J Autism Dev Disord 42, 60–74. https://doi.org/10.1007/s10803-011-1212-2
title: Improvement Rate Difference (IRD) meta-analysis of 24 single-case aided AAC studies
description: This element is the meta-analysis itself: the authors synthesized "Twenty-four single-case studies" on aided AAC with individuals with ASD "via an effect size measure, the Improvement Rate Difference (IRD)." The IRD is used to quantify improvement across single-case designs, a literature base the authors describe as dominated by single-case research "with small numbers of participants." The analysis addressed three research questions concerning overall impact, individual targeted behavioral outcomes, and effects of three types of AAC interventions.
requirements: Requires a corpus of single-case studies amenable to the Improvement Rate Difference effect size measure.
constraints: The underlying research base is single-case research with small numbers of participants, as the article states.
target_learners: individuals with autism spectrum disorders
target_learning_goals: communication skills and other targeted behavioral outcomes supported by aided AAC
examples: The article analyzed 24 single-case studies via the Improvement Rate Difference to answer three research questions about aided AAC effects in ASD.

article_title: Computing of Learner’s Personality Traits Based on Digital Annotations
citation: Omheni, N., Kalboussi, A., Mazhoud, O., & Hadj Kacem, A. (2017). Computing of Learner’s Personality Traits Based on Digital Annotations. International Journal of Artificial Intelligence in Education, 27, 241-267. https://doi.org/10.1007/s40593-016-0124-x
title: i-Read online reading environment with personality profiling from annotations
description: i-Read is an online reading environment where learners upload reading materials, annotate them, and share annotated documents. Its architecture includes a user annotation interface, an annotation analyzer module, a profile constructor module, and three databases with two servers. The analyzer computes six annotation features (total, average, graphical, textual, reference, and compounding annotation counts), and the profile constructor applies multivariate linear regression to estimate Big Five trait scores. The system "offers, besides the traditional annotation functionalities of creation, archiving and sharing, the functionality of readers' personality modeling based on their digital annotation traces."
requirements: Learners must annotate reading materials within the system so that annotation traces can be captured and analyzed.
constraints: The system's regression coefficients were derived from pen-and-paper experiment data, and evaluation focused on conscientiousness and neuroticism only.
target_learners: online learners
higher education students
key_sources: Omheni, N., Kalboussi, A., Mazhoud, O., & Hadj Kacem, A. (2017). Computing of Learner’s Personality Traits Based on Digital Annotations. International Journal of Artificial Intelligence in Education, 27, 241-267. https://doi.org/10.1007/s40593-016-0124-x

article_title: Statistical Techniques to Explore the Quality of Constraints in Constraint-Based Modeling Environments
citation: Gálvez, J., Conejo, R., & Guzmán, E. (2013). Statistical Techniques to Explore the Quality of Constraints in Constraint-Based Modeling Environments. International Journal of Artificial Intelligence in Education. https://doi.org/10.1007/s40593-013-0008-2
title: The IRT+CBM framework treats constraints as psychometric items, enabling data-driven assessment of constraint quality
description: The article proposes a framework that combines Constraint-Based Modeling with Item Response Theory, based on an analogy between constraints and items: both are 'measurement instruments that, though in different environments, collect evidence of knowledge.' A Constraint Characteristic Curve is defined for each constraint, representing the probability of satisfying it as a function of knowledge, allowing IRT mechanisms such as calibration and information analysis to be applied in CBM tutors. The framework replaces heuristic estimates of constraint mastery with a well-founded probabilistic technique.
requirements: A calibration process with prior data from students' performance is needed to estimate CCC parameters before IRT mechanisms can be applied
constraints: If a constraint is always violated or never violated by any student, the information it provides is not relevant for assessment and it only introduces noise
target_learners: students in problem solving learning environments
target_learning_goals: domain principle mastery assessed via constraint satisfaction and violation
key_sources: Gálvez, J., Conejo, R., & Guzmán, E. (2013). Statistical Techniques to Explore the Quality of Constraints in Constraint-Based Modeling Environments. International Journal of Artificial Intelligence in Education. https://doi.org/10.1007/s40593-013-0008-2

article_title: Harmonizing Assistance: Moderating Visual and Textual Aids in AI-Enhanced Textbook Reading with IRead
citation: Xiaoyu Zhang, Vincent Dörig, Peng Cui, Vilém Zouhar, Torbjørn Netland, Mrinmaya Sachan. (2025). Harmonizing Assistance: Moderating Visual and Textual Aids in AI-Enhanced Textbook Reading with IRead. International Journal of Artificial Intelligence in Education. https://doi.org/10.1007/s40593-025-00515-4
title: IRead interactive textbook reading tool
description: IRead is an interactive tool for textbook reading that "uses LLMs with visualization and interaction techniques, to enhance students' reading and learning experiences." It comprises an enhanced textbook reader with highlighting, note-taking, minimap, and search; a hierarchical concept tree visualization with information cards generated by an LLM and refined through human oversight; and Question Wiz, an AI-driven question bot presenting interaction-specific questions. A fuzzy concept mapping technique using sentence-transformer embeddings and cosine similarity links concepts to text terms exceeding a predefined similarity threshold. Its content is produced by a one-time textbook data processing workflow per imported textbook.
requirements: A one-time textbook data processing workflow per textbook, including LLM concept tree generation and question generation model inference
Human oversight to ensure balance of the tree structure and concept quality after autogeneration
constraints: Concept tree generation requires post-inspection because tree balance and concept quality are difficult to consistently manage through the prompt alone
target_learners: higher-education students, from undergraduate to doctorate
examples: In the user study, participants read the first half of the OpenStax chapter 'The Entrepreneurial Perspective' and answered six open-ended questions mapped to Bloom's taxonomy levels
key_sources: Xiaoyu Zhang, Vincent Dörig, Peng Cui, Vilém Zouhar, Torbjørn Netland, Mrinmaya Sachan. (2025). Harmonizing Assistance: Moderating Visual and Textual Aids in AI-Enhanced Textbook Reading with IRead. International Journal of Artificial Intelligence in Education. https://doi.org/10.1007/s40593-025-00515-4

article_title: Learning critical thinking skills online: can precision teaching help?
citation: Ramasamy, S. (2011). An Analysis of Informal Reasoning Fallacy and Critical Thinking Dispositions among Malaysian Undergraduates. Asia e University. https://www.aeu.edu.my
title: Informal Reasoning Fallacy Instrument (IRFI)
description: The IRFI is a 50-item multiple-choice instrument developed by the author to measure whether someone exhibits strong reasoning by being non-fallacious, covering five fallacies (ad hominem, slippery slope, hasty generalization, post hoc, false analogy). It "functions as a Likert scale" via a scoring rubric adopted from Ricco (2007), Neuman (2003) and Weinstock et al (2004): 0 points for falling into the fallacy trap with poor reasoning, 1 for avoiding the trap with reasonable reasoning, and 2 for strong non-fallacious reasoning, giving a 0-100 range with sub-scales of 0-20. Distracters were compiled from students' most frequently generated poor reasoning in an open-ended first phase, and two critical-thinking experts validated content, choices, rubric and language. Overall Cronbach's alpha was .802, though sub-scale reliabilities ranged from .306 (False Analogy) to .593.
requirements: Expert validation of scenarios, response choices, scoring rubric and language by two critical-thinking experts
A scoring rubric distinguishing poor, reasonable and strong reasoning
constraints: Sub-scale reliabilities were low, including .306 for False Analogy and .476 for Hasty Generalization
target_learners: undergraduates
examples: Administered online via surveymonkey.com with no time limit to 259 volunteers, yielding a final sample of 189 after excluding 70 incomplete cases
key_sources: Ramasamy, S. (2011). An Analysis of Informal Reasoning Fallacy and Critical Thinking Dispositions among Malaysian Undergraduates. Asia e University. https://www.aeu.edu.my

article_title: Impact of an educational robot-based intervention on second-graders computational thinking skills: experimental evaluation of the Irûmi program in Paraguay
citation: Emma Näslund-Hadley, Juan Manuel Hernández-Agramonte, Humberto Santos, Pablo Zoido. (2026). Impact of an educational robot-based intervention on second-graders computational thinking skills: experimental evaluation of the Irûmi program in Paraguay. Education Tech Research Dev. https://doi.org/10.1007/s11423-026-10675-2
title: Irûmi educational robot-based CT program for second graders
description: Irûmi ("companion" in Guaraní) is an educational program developed by OMAPA, Paraguay's MEC, and the IDB to develop CT skills in second-grade students. It combines "a curriculum of 18 classroom activities, supported by a technological kit featuring a robot", with teacher training through four workshops and monthly tutor visits. Activities span Disconnected Activities, Familiarization Activities, and Reinforcement and New Topics, using the Smart Robot Albert, 56 coding cards, and erasable navigation boards.
requirements: A second-grade teacher leading activities with support from student assistants, robots distributed at up to three students per robot, and teacher training workshops plus monthly tutor follow-up visits
constraints: Implementation varied across schools: only 69 percent of teachers attended all four workshops, the average number of activities completed was 14.7 of 18, and 25 percent of schools received materials with delay
target_learners: Second-grade students in Paraguayan public primary schools
target_learning_goals: Computational thinking skills including abstraction, algorithmic thinking, and evaluation
examples: Students create a sequence of instructions for the robot, then scan coding cards using the robot's sensors to execute the sequence on a navigation board; classes ran up to three 40-min sessions per week over 11 weeks

Impact of an educational robot-based intervention on second-graders computational thinking skills: experimental evaluation of the Irûmi program in Paraguay. article_title: Exploring the impact of immersive reality for enhancing clinical training in dental education: a systematic review.
citation: Ruslin Muhammad, Sjamsudin Endang, Hanafiah Olivia Avriyanti, Stevanie Carolina, Kurniawan Sri Hastuti, Anshar Muh, Boffano Paolo, Forouzanfar Tymour, Sukotjo Cortino. (2026). Exploring the impact of immersive reality for enhancing clinical training in dental education: a systematic review. BMC Medical Education. https://doi.org/10.1186/s12909-026-09739-x
title: Implement immersive reality as a complement to traditional dental education methods
description: The review recommends integrating immersive reality alongside, not instead of, conventional dental training: "The findings support implementing IR as a complement to traditional dental education methods." The conclusion frames IR as offering "a novel approach to dental education by combining immersive experiences with opportunities for skill development and student engagement". This positions IR simulators as supplementary practice environments that let students repeat procedures safely before clinical contact.
requirements: Institutional capacity for IR hardware and software, since the review states high costs pose barriers and technical maintenance expertise may be unavailable.
constraints: Assessment in the reviewed literature relies heavily on subjective self-reported surveys, which the authors note would be better complemented by quantitative measures like procedural time and error rates.
target_learners: dental students
postgraduates
trainees
examples: The included studies used IR for preclinical pulpotomy, cavity preparation, scaling, suturing and surgical planning training alongside conventional simulator practice.
key_sources: Ruslin Muhammad, Sjamsudin Endang, Hanafiah Olivia Avriyanti, Stevanie Carolina, Kurniawan Sri Hastuti, Anshar Muh, Boffano Paolo, Forouzanfar Tymour, Sukotjo Cortino. (2026). article_title: Registered Dietitians' Knowledge, Attitudes and Use of Simulation-Based Education in Ireland: A Mixed-Methods Study.
citation: A. Power, C. Lee, C. Corish, and A. Shaw. (2026). Registered Dietitians' Knowledge, Attitudes and Use of Simulation‐Based Education in Ireland: A Mixed‐Methods Study. Journal of Human Nutrition and Dietetics. https://doi.org/10.1111/jhn.70326
title: National survey and interview study of Irish dietitians' knowledge, attitudes and use of SBE
description: A convergent mixed-methods study combining an anonymous online SurveyMonkey questionnaire (adapted from previously validated Knowledge–Attitudes–Practice instruments, piloted with three dietitians) with 15 semi-structured Zoom interviews analysed thematically in NVivo. The survey captured "participant characteristics, knowledge and familiarity with SBE, attitudes toward SBE, and current use, barriers and facilitators". Code saturation was reached by interview eight, with all 15 completed to support meaning saturation.
requirements: CORU registration and active practice in Ireland for eligibility
constraints: Snowball sampling may have introduced self-selection bias; the questionnaire itself was not validated
target_learners: CORU-registered dietitians in Ireland
target_learning_goals: understanding educators' knowledge, attitudes and use of simulation-based education
examples: Data collection was open from 30th July to 30th September 2025, yielding 134 responses of which 114 were valid after cleaning
key_sources: A. Power, C. Lee, C. Corish, and A. Shaw. (2026). Registered Dietitians' Knowledge, Attitudes and Use of Simulation‐Based Education in Ireland: A Mixed‐Methods Study. Journal of Human Nutrition and Dietetics. https://doi.org/10.1111/jhn.70326

article_title: Digital Simulation-Based Ultrasound Training for Physiotherapy Students: Prospective Randomized Controlled Trial.
citation: Fernández-Carnero Samuel, Diaz-Pulido Belen, Méndez-Rodriguez Jorge, Pecos-Martin Daniel, Garcia-Miguel Santiago, Achalandabaso-Ochoa Alexander, Cuenca-Zaldívar Nicolas, Naranjo-Cinto Sr Fermín. (2026). Digital Simulation–Based Ultrasound Training for Physiotherapy Students: Prospective Randomized Controlled Trial. JMIR Medical Education. https://doi.org/10.2196/87897
title: Item response theory using a Rasch model for evaluating ultrasound competency assessment
description: The article applies item response theory using a 1-parameter Rasch model to estimate item difficulty and student ability in a practical ultrasound assessment. The authors state that "The application of the 1-parameter Rasch model proved to be a robust methodological choice for this cohort (n=68); its mathematical parsimony allowed for stable and reliable estimates of item difficulty and student proficiency even in samples of modest size." The framework requires assumptions of unidimensionality, local independence, and parameter invariance.
requirements: Unidimensionality of items
local independence of items
invariance of item parameters across subgroups
constraints: Generalizability and global scalability of the instrument remain to be confirmed in multicenter studies
target_learners: physiotherapy students
examples: The study verified model assumptions including nonsignificant T1m statistics for unidimensionality and nonsignificant Andersen likelihood ratio test for parameter invariance

(2026). Digital Simulation–Based Ultrasound Training for Physiotherapy Students: Prospective Randomized Controlled Trial. JMIR Medical Education. https://doi.org/10.2196/87897

article_title: Interpretation of course conceptual structure and student self-efficacy: an integrated strategy of knowledge graphs with item response modeling.
citation: Cao Zhen-Yu, Lin Feng, Feng Chun. (2024). Interpretation of course conceptual structure and student self-efficacy: an integrated strategy of knowledge graphs with item response modeling. BMC Medical Education. https://doi.org/10.1186/s12909-024-05401-6
title: Integrated IRT and knowledge graph modeling framework for quantitatively assessing difficulty, importance, and necessity of course knowledge points
description: The article proposes combining item response modeling with knowledge graph modeling to quantify properties of knowledge points from student self-rated difficulty data. IRT places person ability (SEL) and item difficulty on the same logit scale, addressing "which KPs demand additional teaching resources", while the KGM built on partial correlations identifies important and necessary points, addressing "which KPs need to be taught first". The article states "The IRT and KG methods utilized in this study offer distinct perspectives for visualizing hierarchical relationships and correlations among the KPs". The framework was validated on real-world teaching data from a physical therapy course.
requirements: A difficulty-rating questionnaire on course knowledge points administered to students, with KPs selected by expert panel
Sequential npIRT (Mokken) then parametric IRT modeling, plus GGMncv network modeling with backbone extraction
constraints: Item difficulty meaning depends on the binarization strategy, reflecting difficulty of being self-confident about mastering KPs
The KG reflects difficulty correlations under the influence of SEL and may not exactly mirror students' knowledge schemas
target_learners: Higher education students in rehabilitation/physical therapy courses
target_learning_goals: Identifying difficult, important, and necessary knowledge points to customize teaching plans and learning objectives
examples: The pipeline was applied to 100 KPs from the Therapeutic Exercise course rated by 208 students, producing a 50-item 3PLM and a 58-node KG main component
key_sources: Cao Zhen-Yu, Lin Feng, Feng Chun. (2024). Interpretation of course conceptual structure and student self-efficacy: an integrated strategy of knowledge graphs with item response modeling. BMC Medical Education. https://doi.org/10.1186/s12909-024-05401-6

article_title: Computer Adaptive vs. Non-adaptive Medical Progress Testing: Feasibility, Test Performance, and Student Experiences.
citation: Van Wijk EV, Donkers J, De Laat PCJ, Meiboom AA, Jacobs B, Ravesloot JH, Tio RA, Van Der Vleuten CPM, Langers AMJ, Bremers AJA. (2024). Computer Adaptive vs. Non-adaptive Medical Progress Testing: Feasibility, Test Performance, and Student Experiences. Perspectives on Medical Education. https://doi.org/10.5334/pme.1345
title: Item Response Theory (IRT) as the psychometric basis of computer adaptive testing, contrasted with Classical Test Theory
description: The article frames computerized adaptive testing on plain Item Response Theory, which "uses mathematical models to estimate the underlying ability level ('theta') of the test-taker based on their responses to different items", with each item characterized by difficulty and discrimination parameters. This contrasts with Classical Test Theory, the basis of the conventional fixed linear PT, which assumes the observed total score equals true ability with identical measurement error for all scores, potentially yielding less precise ability estimates.
requirements: A pre-calibrated item bank with item difficulty and discrimination parameters estimated under a Rasch model
constraints: The article notes other forms of computer adaptive testing exist (multidimensional, content-based, testlet-based, tree-based), each with their own assumptions, merits, and limitations; this article's focus is plain IRT-based CAT
target_learners: medical students across all years of a six-year curriculum
target_learning_goals: accurate estimation of student ability level for progress-testing decisions
examples: The CA-PT in this study calibrated 3400 questions from 30 historical linear progress tests following a Rasch model to obtain item difficulties
key_sources: Van Wijk EV, Donkers J, De Laat PCJ, Meiboom AA, Jacobs B, Ravesloot JH, Tio RA, Van Der Vleuten CPM, Langers AMJ, Bremers AJA. (2024). Computer Adaptive vs. Non-adaptive Medical Progress Testing: Feasibility, Test Performance, and Student Experiences. Perspectives on Medical Education. https://doi.org/10.5334/pme.1345
